findings.headline: Pension fund has written off overpayments and is working to recover further outstanding overpayment funds
findings.detail: The fund wrote off £868.90 in Q1 due to duplicate payments to a pensioner and overpayments to deceased members. The document notes ongoing work to recover 'further outstanding overpayment funds', suggesting a backlog of unrecovered overpayments.
findings.matters: Overpayment write-offs and recovery issues indicate control weaknesses in pension administration and represent financial losses absorbed by the fund; ongoing recovery efforts suggest a systemic problem rather than isolated incidents
findings.figures: £868.90 written off in Q1
findings.quote: The Fund has had to write off approx. £868.90 in Q1 due to overpaid pensions from deceased members and an overpayment in respect of an admin error of duplicate payments to a pensioner.

findings.headline: Helpdesk service performance deteriorated in Q1 with longer wait times and higher call abandonment
findings.detail: Call waiting time increased from 3 minutes 17 seconds in Q4 to 4 minutes 35 seconds in Q1. Call abandonment rates peaked at 5.4% during the quarter and ended at 4.4%, both increases from the prior quarter.
findings.matters: Degrading service metrics during a period of stated resource constraints could indicate that the council's outsourced pension administration is beginning to strain under demand, risking further member dissatisfaction and operational failures
findings.figures: 3 minutes 17 seconds (Q4) vs 4 minutes 35 seconds (Q1); peak abandonment 5.4%, ending period at 4.4%
findings.quote: The average call waiting time rose in Q1 to 4minutes 35 compared to 3 minutes 17 in Q4. The call abandonment rate also rose during the quarter to a peak of 5.4% ending the period at 4.4%.

findings.headline: Pension administration service faces resource constraints that are slowing resolution of issues
findings.detail: The paper identifies 'limited resources' as a key challenge for the administering authority (LPPA). Combined with complex legislation and data management demands, this means some issues will take months or years to resolve.
findings.matters: Under-resourced pension administration could compromise the council's ability to meet regulatory obligations (such as McCloud remedies or Pensions Dashboard connectivity) and could create financial exposure if issues are not resolved promptly
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Challenges include increasing complex legislation, managing data, limited resources and difficulty in engaging with employers, which mean some issues will take months or years to resolve fully.

findings.headline: Member dissatisfaction is increasing, particularly for members going through deferred retirement
findings.detail: The paper reports that dissatisfaction among pension members has increased in Q1. Members in the deferred retirement process showed particularly poor experience, with low survey completion rates and documented dissatisfaction with their member experience.
findings.matters: Rising dissatisfaction with a critical council service could lead to member complaints, regulatory scrutiny from the Pensions Regulator, and potentially require council investment to remediate service quality issues
findings.figures: Most members in Q1 going through deferred retirements process were dissatisfied with their member experience
findings.quote: Member satisfaction survey responses remain low and dissatisfaction has increased. Most members in Q1 going through the deferred retirements process did not complete a survey and were dissatisfied to their member experience.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Fund completed transition from active to passive global equity management, consolidating to Legal & General and BlackRock mandates
findings.detail: The committee approved and executed a strategic shift away from active management through the LCIV Morgan Stanley Fund to fully passive equity structures. This transition simplifies the fund's structure and reduces management costs while maintaining broad market exposure. Investment management expenses fell slightly from £6.74m in 2024/25 to £6.68m in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Lower investment management costs improve fund efficiency and reduce the net cost to employers; passive management also typically provides more transparent and predictable investment structuring
findings.figures: Management fees: £6.0m (2025/26); transaction costs £0.6m; total investment management expenses £6.68m down from £6.74m
findings.quote: During the year the Committee approved significant changes to the Fund's equity portfolio, agreeing to redeem the Fund's investment in the LCIV Morgan Stanley Fund and transition fully to passive equity management. This resulted in assets being invested through the Fund's existing Legal & General Investment Management mandate and a new BlackRock Authorised Contractual Scheme (ACS) fund, simplifying the Fund's equity structure while continuing to provide broad market exposure at a lower cost.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Fund investment performance lagged the average LGPS return by 5.43% in 2025/26, returning 3.5% versus peer average
findings.detail: While the fund outperformed its own strategic benchmark by 0.54%, it underperformed the average Local Government Pension Scheme fund significantly. This could indicate either that the fund's strategic benchmark is conservative, or that investment returns are below peer standard. If this trend continues, it could put upward pressure on future employer contribution rates.
findings.matters: Persistent investment underperformance could necessitate higher council contributions to maintain funding levels, representing a material future financial commitment
findings.figures: 2025/26 return: 3.5%; average LGPS return: 5.43% higher; outperformance vs strategic benchmark: 0.54%
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the Fund's investment performance was 3.5% (3.7% in 2024/35) to £1.48bn. This was below the average LGPS return by -5.43%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Pension fund funding level improved to 113% with a £161m surplus, up from 105% in the prior valuation
findings.detail: The 2025 triennial actuarial valuation confirms the fund's strong financial position. This improvement means the council's future pension contribution requirements are likely to remain sustainable. A surplus of this scale at the fund level reduces pressure on employer contribution rates going forward.
findings.matters: A well-funded pension scheme reduces the future financial burden on the council and means contribution rates can remain affordable; this is material to lenders assessing long-term financial stability
findings.figures: 113% funding level (2025 valuation), £161m surplus, compared to 105% funding level (2022 valuation)
findings.quote: The valuation confirmed the Fund's strong financial position, with assets sufficient to meet 113% of accrued liabilities, representing a surplus of approximately £161 million and an improvement from the 105% funding level achieved at the 2022 valuation.

findings.headline: The fund has introduced index-linked gilts to better match inflation-linked pension liabilities.
findings.detail: Since the 2023 strategic review, the fund has dedicated an allocation to index-linked government bonds to improve alignment between its assets and the inflation-linked nature of its pension obligations. This reduces the risk that pension liabilities will grow faster than asset returns if inflation rises.
findings.matters: Inflation is a material liability risk for the council. Rising inflation increases the present value of future pension payments, and this change shows active risk management to hedge that exposure.
findings.figures: Allocation to UK Government Bonds (index-linked): 5% +/- 5% of total strategic asset allocation.
findings.quote: A dedicated allocation to index-linked gilts has been introduced since the 2023 strategic asset allocation, to improve the alignment between the Fund's assets and its inflation-linked liabilities.

findings.headline: The pension fund is now cashflow negative, with benefit payments exceeding contributions.
findings.detail: The fund has crossed a structural threshold: it no longer receives more in employer and member contributions than it pays out in pensions. Instead, it must draw down assets to meet ongoing benefit payments. This represents a permanent shift in the fund's cash position and means the strong funding surplus (currently £161m) will gradually deplete to cover the gap.
findings.matters: A pension fund consuming rather than generating cash means the council must find liquidity elsewhere to service growing pension liabilities, constraining the council's financial flexibility and increasing the reserve drawdown rate over time.
findings.figures: As at 31 March 2025: Funding Level 113%, Assets £1,413m, Liabilities £1,252m, Surplus £161m. Cashflow Position: Negative.
findings.quote: The Fund is now cashflow negative, with benefit payments exceeding contributions.

findings.headline: VAT partial exemption breach would cost council £3m annually; identified as active risk on capital projects
findings.detail: The council has identified a material risk that breach of VAT partial exemption thresholds (driven by capital project composition) would trigger approximately £3m in annual costs to the council. Finance officers are actively monitoring capital projects to manage this risk, but it remains an unresolved exposure.
findings.matters: £3m annual cost is material to revenue position. This is not hypothetical—it is a specific identified exposure that could crystallize. For a finance director, it represents a financial risk that requires active management.
findings.figures: Potential VAT breach cost: £3m per year
findings.quote: A breach would likely cost the Council around £3m per year whilst in breach.

findings.headline: Civic Campus flagship project delayed by contractor; £2.8m slippage on Town Hall refurbishment
findings.detail: The Civic Campus redevelopment (the largest single capital project at £23.5m spend in 2025-26) experienced delays from the works contractor. The Town Hall refurbishment element saw £2.8m slip from 2025-26 into 2026-27. Commercial units acquisition delayed by a further £2m. This is the council's most visible regeneration project and slippage suggests execution challenges.
findings.matters: Project delays on flagship investments raise questions about procurement, contract management, and ability to deliver on schedule. For a lender, delays on high-profile projects signal broader execution risk and may indicate cost overruns to follow.
findings.figures: Civic Campus total outturn 2025-26: £23.5m vs Q3 budget £29.3m; Town Hall refurbishment slippage: £2.8m; Commercial units slippage: £2m
findings.quote: Civic Campus saw £2.8m on the Town Hall refurbishment slip into 2026/27 due to delays by the works contractor and £2m on the Acquisition of Commercial Units now anticipated in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account borrowing increased by £100.274m in a single year to £559.187m
findings.detail: The HRA CFR (self-contained housing account borrowing) grew from £458.913m (2024-25 closing) to £559.187m (2025-26 closing), an increase of £100.274m. Although forecast to reduce slightly to £534.867m by 2029-30, the single-year spike is substantial. HRA accounts are self-financing with strict debt limits; large increases narrow headroom for future investment or refinancing.
findings.matters: Rapid HRA borrowing growth constrains future investment capacity and refinancing flexibility. For a lender, large single-year increases signal acceleration in housing delivery that must be sustained or the HRA faces debt service pressure.
findings.figures: HRA CFR 2024-25 closing: £458.913m; 2025-26 closing: £559.187m (£100.274m increase); forecast 2029-30: £534.867m
findings.quote: The 2025/26 closing HRA CFR is £559.187m, this is an increase of £100.274m in comparison to 2024/25.

findings.headline: General Fund borrowing requirement increased by £32m in one year, forecast to grow to £309.83m by 2029-30
findings.detail: The General Fund Headline CFR (Capital Financing Requirement) reached £237.78m at end of 2025-26, an in-year net increase of £32m. The council forecasts this will grow to £309.83m by end of 2029-30. The council explicitly states this growth 'puts additional pressures on revenue budgets', meaning future years will spend more on debt servicing (MRP and interest) at the expense of service delivery.
findings.matters: Rising CFR reduces revenue flexibility and increases leverage. For a lender, accelerating borrowing with no offsetting revenue growth signals deteriorating debt capacity. Each £1 of additional CFR requires ongoing revenue to service it.
findings.figures: GF Headline CFR 2025/26: £237.78m (in-year increase £32m); forecast 2029/30: £309.83m; annual MRP charges range £2.8m-£4.1m
findings.quote: The General Fund Headline CFR (excluding the self-financing schemes) is £237.78m as at the end of 2025/26, an in-year net increase of £32m, and is forecast to increase to £309.83m by the end of 2029/30. The increase in GF Headline CFR puts additional pressures on revenue budgets.

findings.headline: Finance and Corporate Services delivered only 60.3% of savings with £750k pushed to 2026-27
findings.detail: Finance and Corporate Services achieved £760k of £1.260m savings target, delivering only 60.3%. The largest shortfall is the organisational review of senior chief officer structures, where only £250k of a £750k target was delivered, with savings pushed to 2026-27. This shows the council is struggling to deliver planned corporate efficiencies.
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls in corporate services indicate the council's ability to deliver planned efficiencies is at risk. Deferring savings to next year when operational pressures continue growing compounds future budget risk.
findings.figures: FCS target £1.260m; FCS achieved £760k; delivery 60.3%; organisational review target £750k, achieved £250k, £500k shortfall
findings.quote: An organisational review of the senior chief officer structures of the Council – savings will be delivered in 2026/27.

findings.headline: HRA disrepairs compensation claims nearly tripled budget at £1.868m overspend
findings.detail: S82 disrepairs compensation claims cost £2.513m against a budget of £0.645m, representing a £1.868m or 190% variance. The report cites high claim volumes and associated legal costs as the cause. This is a material unbudgeted liability on the housing stock.
findings.matters: Disrepair claims represent a significant legal and financial liability on the HRA. High volumes indicate either deteriorating asset condition or residents becoming more willing to pursue claims, either of which threatens HRA financial stability.
findings.figures: Budget £645k; outturn £2,513k; overspend £1,868k (290% of budget)
findings.quote: S82 Disrepairs Compensation 645 1,868 High claim volumes and associated legal costs

findings.headline: DSG High Needs cumulative deficit of £7.882m dependent on DfE funding decision in Autumn 2026
findings.detail: The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has increased to £7.882m in 2025-26 under the safety valve recovery plan agreed with Department for Education. The council anticipates £7.581m in High Needs Stability Grant funding, but this is explicitly stated to be 'to be confirmed in Autumn 2026'. If not provided in full, the council faces unplanned costs to cover the £0.381m residual deficit plus any shortfall.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liability dependent entirely on a DfE funding decision five months away. If the anticipated stability grant is not provided or is reduced, it represents an unbudgeted call on the council's resources.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £7.882m; anticipated stability grant £7.581m; residual deficit to be covered by local authority £0.381m
findings.quote: In accordance with the Council's DSG HNB safety valve recovery plan, agreed with the Department for Education (DfE), the cumulative deficit has increased to £7.882m in 2025/26. DfE have indicated potential significant extra funding through the High Needs Stability Grant with respect to this retained deficit, to be confirmed in Autumn 2026.

findings.headline: Adult and Children's social care support costs overspent by £7.8m due to growing resident complexity and numbers
findings.detail: Supported Living and Extra Care overspent £4.505m on care packages for residents with complex learning disabilities, mental health needs, and physical support. Direct Payments overspent £1.441m due to increased residents supported. Children Looked After placements overspent £1.9m on additional high needs support, secure welfare and independent fostering. These are driven by demographic pressures and increasing acuity of need.
findings.matters: Recurrent overspends in social care indicate the council cannot adequately budget for aging population pressures and increased complexity. These costs typically escalate year-on-year and are difficult to control.
findings.figures: Supported Living and Extra Care £4.505m overspend; Direct Payments £1.441m overspend; Children LAC placements £1.9m overspend; combined £7.846m
findings.quote: Overspends relating to care and support packages for residents with complex Learning Disabilities, residents with mental health needs placed in supported living placements and residents with Physical Support needs [and] Children Looked After and Care Leavers placements additional expenditure is £1.9m (this includes additional high needs support packages, secure welfare, independent fostering agency)

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend of £4.5m combining general fund and HRA pressures
findings.detail: General Fund Housing Solutions overspent £3.256m on temporary accommodation for homeless households, described as additional expenditure common across London boroughs. HRA separately overspent £1.275m on decants driving temporary accommodation and disturbance allowance costs. Combined, this represents a significant and growing recurrent cost pressure not yet controlled.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is structurally growing faster than budgeted, indicating both rising homelessness and the council's inability to secure permanent housing. This is a recurrent cost that will persist and likely grow.
findings.figures: GF Housing Solutions overspend £3.256m; HRA decants overspend £1.275m; combined overspend £4.531m
findings.quote: Additional expenditure (in common with other London Boroughs) in providing accommodation for homeless households (mainly private landlords and bed and breakfast hotels) [and] A high level of decants is driving a forecast overspend in temporary accommodation and disturbance allowance costs of £1.3m.

findings.headline: Underlying service overspends of £9.7m masked by contingency use and one-off technical savings
findings.detail: Departments overspent by £9.706m in total. The council achieved overall balance by drawing £7.509m from corporate contingencies and gaining £8.492m from central budget underspends. The largest of these underspends (£5.223m) came from net borrowing costs due to higher-than-budgeted cash returns. The report explicitly states underlying overspends remain in demand-led services and that 'there remain significant ongoing risks of rising costs and demand'.
findings.matters: The balanced outturn depends on one-time use of contingency and technical items (improved cash returns, lower depreciation) that will not recur, leaving structural departmental overspends of nearly £10m exposed.
findings.figures: Total departmental overspend £9.706m; centrally managed budget underspend £8.492m; net borrowing costs underspend £5.223m; corporate contingency drawn £7.509m
findings.quote: Although a net underspend has been delivered, underlying overspends remain, especially in front line and demand led services due to demographic change and the long term national economic conditions. Whilst provision for growth and inflation has been included in many of these budgets for 2025/26, there remain significant ongoing risks of rising costs and demand and complexity of that demand that will need to be managed to achieve a balanced outturn for 2025/26.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account debt dominance increased further: now 89.33% of council's total external debt
findings.detail: Of £495.8m total borrowing, £442.9m services housing. HRA Capital Financing Requirement grew £100.3m in one year (from £458.9m to £559.2m), meaning future housing service budgets must absorb growing finance costs or pass them to tenants.
findings.matters: High concentration of debt in HRA (a captive customer base with limited exit options) limits financial flexibility. Rapid HRA debt growth means rent pressures or budget cuts to housing services are likely.
findings.figures: HRA debt £442.9m of £495.8m total (89.33%); HRA CFR growth £458.9m → £559.2m
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) is responsible for servicing 89.33% of the Council's external debt and the General Fund is responsible for the remaining 10.67%.

findings.headline: Council relies on cash reserves to fund capital projects (internal borrowing of £116.1m) rather than external market borrowing
findings.detail: HRA's Capital Financing Requirement of £559m is only £442.9m externally borrowed. The £116.1m gap is funded from cash balances held on the balance sheet, reducing the council's available liquidity buffer for operations and emergencies.
findings.matters: Using cash to fund capital signals reliance on cash generation or balance sheet reserves rather than access to capital markets. This reduces financial flexibility and resilience against cash flow disruption.
findings.figures: HRA CFR £559m; HRA external debt £442.9m; internal borrowing £116.1m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Council had an under-borrowed position. This means that past and future capital expenditure is not fully funded by capital resources, with the balance instead being financed by cash balances (known as internal borrowing).

findings.headline: Net borrowing increased by £207.5m in one year; total debt nearly doubled from £288m to £495.8m
findings.detail: Council borrowed £227.5m net (after £19.95m repayments), increasing total borrowing by 72% in a single year. Simultaneously, average interest rate rose from 3.75% to 3.91%, increasing annual debt servicing costs. HRA (housing) debt grew from £237.4m to £442.9m, a 86% increase.
findings.matters: Rapid debt growth combined with rising interest rates signals accelerating debt service burden. Lenders assess whether interest costs are sustainable relative to revenue; trajectory matters as much as absolute position.
findings.quote: During the year, the Council repaid £19.95m in loans across the PWLB and CMI. The Council also took out £227.5m of loans with the PWLB. This took borrowing from £288m at the beginning of the financial year to £495.8m at the end.

findings.headline: Council breached two prudential indicators: Capital Financing Requirement and short-term debt maturity
findings.detail: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement reached £897m against an approved limit of £856m (£41m over). The proportion of debt maturing within 12 months reached 17% against a maximum permitted of 15%, concentrating refinancing risk in the near term. These are statutory limits under the Prudential Code.
findings.matters: Prudential indicator breaches indicate the council is operating outside regulatory constraints. The CFR breach suggests capital expenditure is unsustainable relative to planned resources; the maturity breach concentrates refinancing risk and increases exposure to rate movements.
findings.figures: CFR: £897m vs £856m limit; short-term maturity: 17% vs 15% maximum
findings.quote: The Council operated according to the Treasury Limits and Prudential Indicators during 2025/26, meeting all but two prudential indicators.

findings.paper_title: Four Year Capital Programme 2026-30 and Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: VAT partial exemption threshold breach would create £2m annual cost exposure if mitigation fails.
findings.detail: The council faces a known VAT partial exemption risk. If the 5% partial exemption limit is breached without HMRC mitigation, all VAT incurred on exempt activities in that year cannot be reclaimed, creating a £2m cost impact. Capital transactions represent the largest risk to this threshold. The document notes that unanticipated expense or project slippages can present challenges.
findings.matters: A discrete £2m annual cost risk that could materialise if capital delivery slips or commercial transactions accelerate.
findings.figures: VAT breach cost: approximately £2m per year
findings.quote: If this threshold is breached without HMRC mitigation, then all VAT incurred in support of exempt activities, in that year, can no longer be reclaimed from HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) and becomes payable by the Council. This would represent a cost of approximately £2m per year of breach.

findings.paper_title: Four Year Capital Programme 2026-30 and Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Fair Funding framework rehaul reduces General Fund capital capacity and will constrain future investment beyond 2026/27.
findings.detail: The government's Fair Funding framework, which will overhaul local authority funding regime, is expected to materially reduce the council's ability to finance capital investment. The General Fund capital programme is already reducing significantly after the Civic Campus completes, and a wider review of the capital programme is scheduled for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Government funding reform creates uncertainty over medium-term capital investment capacity and signals constrained resources.
findings.quote: The Council's General Fund 2026/27 revenue budget report explains how the Council is being impacted by the Government's implementation of the Fair Funding framework, which comprehensively overhauls the funding regime that runs to 2025/26. This will have an impact on the Council's ability to finance capital investment into the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Four Year Capital Programme 2026-30 and Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Civic Campus £64m commercial investment is dependent on rental income to repay initial costs over 45 years, with income not yet secured.
findings.detail: The council has committed £64m to acquire commercial units as part of the Civic Campus regeneration. The strategy explicitly relies on securing tenants to pay rent sufficient to repay the investment over 45 years. The paper states negotiations have begun but no leases are signed. Income flow is essential to the council's financial strategy but remains unproven.
findings.matters: A material capital investment and revenue forecasting assumption dependent on commercial lettings in uncertain market conditions.
findings.figures: £64m capital budget for commercial unit acquisition; 45-year repayment period
findings.quote: A capital budget of £64m was approved for the acquisition of commercial units that will be constructed by the LLP as part of the Civic Campus Programme. For each of the buildings, the Council will then secure lessees paying rent to the Council, covering the cost of the acquisition over 45 years. Negotiations have already begun with potential occupiers for some of the commercial spaces.

findings.paper_title: Four Year Capital Programme 2026-30 and Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA capital financing requirement forecast to rise to £670.2m, with £116.9m new borrowing over four years and no scheduled debt repayment.
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's capital financing requirement is forecast to increase from £563.3m to £670.2m by end of 2029/30. Over the four-year programme, the HRA will borrow £116.9m with no planned debt repayment, indicating escalating HRA debt dependency. This is set against uncertain revenue generation from housing development schemes.
findings.matters: Rising HRA debt without repayment pathway suggests deteriorating financial sustainability of the housing account.
findings.figures: HRA CFR opening: £563.3m; HRA CFR closing: £670.2m; new HRA borrowing 2027/28-2029/30: £116.9m
findings.quote: The HRA CFR is forecast to rise to £670.2m by the end of the four year budget period.

findings.paper_title: Four Year Capital Programme 2026-30 and Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing costs have more than tripled from 1.5% in December 2021 to 4.65%, materially increasing debt service burden.
findings.detail: With long-term PWLB rates now at 4.65% compared to 1.5% three years ago, the council's cost of borrowing has more than trebled. The council plans to borrow £192.2m across the capital programme, with £116.9m of this for HRA investment, making interest rate movements a substantial financial pressure on both revenue and HRA accounts.
findings.matters: A fundamental shift in the cost of capital reduces financial flexibility and increases long-term debt service obligations.
findings.figures: PWLB rate: 4.65% (now) vs 1.5% (December 2021); BoE rate: 3.75%; total planned borrowing: £192.2m
findings.quote: For the council, as it borrows primarily from the Public Works Loans Board (PWLB), this interest rate regarding long-term borrowing now stands at 4.65% compared to 1.5% in December 2021.

findings.paper_title: Four Year Capital Programme 2026-30 and Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Hammersmith Bridge represents an unfunded liability with £2m annual maintenance costs and £20.2m government funding still owed.
findings.detail: The council has spent £54m to date on bridge stabilisation and pre-restoration works. The government and TfL have contributed only £15.9m despite an earlier commitment to fund two-thirds (expected £36.4m). The council incurs £2m annually to keep the bridge safe and maintain pedestrian/cycle functions. Full restoration funding is uncertain, with the council's contribution dependent on tolling or road user charging schemes that lack government support.
findings.matters: A material unfunded liability extending beyond the 4-year programme, with ongoing revenue drain and restoration costs unresolved.
findings.figures: £54m spent to date; £36.4m government share (two-thirds); £15.9m received so far (DfT £13.0m + TfL £2.9m); £20.2m owed; £2m annual ongoing costs
findings.quote: Even without funding from DfT and/ or TfL to proceed with further restoration works, the council is incurring ongoing costs of approximately £2m a year to safely maintain and keep the bridge open for pedestrians, cyclists and river traffic.

findings.headline: PWLB borrowing costs at risk of 0.4% increase if HRA certainty rate not extended beyond April 2026
findings.detail: The council is monitoring whether the HRA certainty rate for Public Works Loan Board borrowing will continue beyond April 2026. Loss of this rate would mean General Fund borrowing reverts to higher rates, increasing debt servicing costs across the capital programme.
findings.matters: A 0.4% increase in borrowing costs on the council's capital programme creates material additional annual debt servicing expense.
findings.figures: 0.4% favourable position under HRA certainty rate versus General Fund borrowing
findings.quote: Monitoring of whether HRA certainty rate for PWLB borrowing will be extended from April 2026, which gives a 0.4% favourable position over General Fund borrowing

findings.headline: Adult Social Care Transformation programme resource requirements unfunded in future years
findings.detail: Implementation costs for the new ASC operational service model are expected to require resource investment beyond the transformation funding already deployed. 2026/27 costs are to be covered from Policy Contingencies; funding for future years remains unresolved and to be discussed further.
findings.matters: Reliance on contingency reserves to fund transformation in 2026/27, with unclear funding for subsequent years, signals potential draw on reserves and deferred budget solutions.
findings.figures: None provided; 2026/27 from contingency reserve, future years undefined
findings.quote: 2026/27 anticipated to be funded from Policy Contingencies and for future years to be discussed further.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand forecast to increase by 250 additional households above budget
findings.detail: Beyond the baseline TA forecast, the council faces risk of 250 additional households requiring emergency temporary accommodation this year. This drives material growth in the council's most expensive housing provision, with mitigation focused on increasing access to private rented housing.
findings.matters: TA provision is expensive; 250 additional households materially increases housing and support service costs.
findings.figures: 250 additional households above current forecast
findings.quote: There is a risk of a further increase in the number of households in Temporary Accommodation - based on an additional 250 households this year above the current forecast

findings.headline: Cyber security incident creates unquantified short and medium-term cost liabilities
findings.detail: The council was affected by a cyber security incident in December 2025 through joint working with neighbouring authorities. The council states that short and medium-term cost implications are anticipated but will be quantified and reported separately in future.
findings.matters: Unquantified cost risk to the council from a recent incident; lenders require visibility of ultimate cost and recovery position.
findings.figures: None provided; costs to be assessed and reported
findings.quote: It is likely that there will be short and medium cost implications and these will be assessed and reported in the future.

findings.headline: Fair Funding framework reductions will constrain council's ability to deliver current service range
findings.detail: Government's Fair Funding framework is reducing the council's general fund allocation. The council explicitly acknowledges this will impact its organisational capacity to deliver all currently provided functions and is developing alternative funding strategies.
findings.matters: General funding reductions directly constrain financial capacity and may require service prioritisation or withdrawal.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Reductions in funding as a result of Government's Fair Funding framework for the General Fund will have an impact on the organisation's ability to deliver all the functions it currently provides.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care provider costs forecast to exceed 3.2% budget provision due to Employment Rights Bill
findings.detail: Care provider inflation pressures are expected to outstrip the 3.2% inflationary increase assumed in the budget. Cost growth drivers include London Living Wage requirements and the unquantified impact of the Employment Rights Bill on care provider staffing costs, amplified by a significant recommissioning programme.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is non-discretionary statutory spending with growing demand; unbudgeted cost overruns cannot be avoided and directly reduce council's capacity to meet care act duties.
findings.figures: 3.2% inflationary assumption in budget; actual pressures unquantified but expected to exceed this
findings.quote: We may see further cost pressures in the ASC care market to cover increases in London Living wages and the unquantified Employment Rights Bill will mean greater pressures than the 3.2% inflationary increase proposed in the budget

findings.headline: Hammersmith Bridge capital project at financial risk; accumulated costs may revert to revenue if funding fails
findings.detail: Bridge strengthening and restoration works are proceeding at risk pending confirmation of funding contributions from Department for Transport and Transport for London. If the full project does not proceed, accumulated capital expenditure to date must be charged to revenue budget. Additional ongoing maintenance costs may also require revenue funding.
findings.matters: Material capital expenditure could become an unexpected one-off revenue charge if funding partners withdraw, creating material budget pressure.
findings.figures: None provided; amount accumulated to date unspecified
findings.quote: If the full strengthening and restoration project does not go ahead, some capital costs to date may need to be charged back to revenue. There may also be additional ongoing maintenance costs that will require funding.

findings.headline: Ringfenced DSG deficit as high needs cost growth outpaces funding allocation
findings.detail: Despite successful early intervention transformation, the council's high needs spending continues to exceed dedicated schools grant funding growth year on year. This creates a baseline structural deficit in a ringfenced budget that cannot be offset from general reserves or council borrowing.
findings.matters: Ongoing structural deficit in ringfenced high needs funding reduces financial flexibility and may require cumulative reserve contributions or external support.
findings.figures: None provided; described as baseline pressure continuing to grow
findings.quote: Despite the success of the Council's early intervention transformation programme, cost growth continues to outstrip funding allocation growth. There is subsequently a baseline DSG pressure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G – Reserves strategy and forecast
findings.headline: No capital receipts forecast; limits financial flexibility for planned investment
findings.detail: The council forecasts nil capital receipts to 2028/29. This removes a traditional lever for funding investment and means the council cannot use asset sales to fund priorities or reduce reserve draw.
findings.matters: Capital receipt generation is typically a means to ease budget pressure; its absence means reserves must fund all planned investment and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £0m forecasted capital receipts
findings.quote: There is currently a nil future forecast for General Fund receipts.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G – Reserves strategy and forecast
findings.headline: £5.1m annual savings assumed in budget with only partial reserve protection if unachieved
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget assumes £5.1m of in-year savings. The strategy acknowledges that if only 50% of these savings materialise, the shortfall would need to be met from the Corporate Demands and Pressures reserve—meaning 50% failure leaves a £2.55m shortfall with no identified backup.
findings.matters: A lender assessing budget stability needs to know that the council's budget has a structural dependency on £5.1m of savings with limited contingency for failure.
findings.figures: £5.1m in-year savings plans for 2025/26; shortfall of 50% (£2.55m) would exceed identified reserve cover
findings.quote: In year savings plans of £5.1m are assumed in the 2025/26 budget. If 50% of the target became unachievable, the shortfall could be met by the Corporate Demands and Pressure reserve in the short term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G – Reserves strategy and forecast
findings.headline: £5m reserve held against write-off risk if planned capital schemes do not proceed
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that pre-development costs for capital schemes may need to be written off if those schemes are not taken forward. A £5m reserve has been established specifically to mitigate this risk, suggesting material uncertainty about capital project delivery.
findings.matters: Pre-development costs that cannot be recouped represent a direct drain on reserves and signal uncertainty in the capital strategy's execution.
findings.figures: £5m Pre-Development reserve
findings.quote: Any write-off of pre-development costs should it not be possible to take forward planned capital schemes - the updated reserves strategy incorporates an earmarked reserve of £5m as mitigation against this risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G – Reserves strategy and forecast
findings.headline: £14.55m Dedicated Schools Grant high needs deficit dependent on government recovery funding
findings.detail: The council holds a £14.55m earmarked reserve to offset a cumulative DSG deficit. The stated plan to reduce this depends on the council securing additional government funding and executing a recovery plan. Failure would require sustained reserve draw.
findings.matters: This is a material contingent liability that limits the council's actual financial headroom and whose resolution depends on central government action beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: £14.55m cumulative DSG high needs deficit as at April 2025
findings.quote: An earmarked reserve of £14.55m is held as at April 2025 regarding the cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) high needs deficit. The deficit is expected to reduce in future years following the Council securing additional government funding and continuing to manage its DSG recovery plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G – Reserves strategy and forecast
findings.headline: Hammersmith Bridge costs incurred without confirmed government funding
findings.detail: The council is actively incurring both revenue and capital costs for Hammersmith Bridge while awaiting government confirmation of funding. This creates a contingent liability with no certainty of cost recovery. The 2025/26 budget includes £1.7m provision for Bridge-related costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council is exposed to potentially unrecoverable costs on a major capital project if government funding is not confirmed.
findings.figures: £1.7m provision for costs related to Hammersmith Bridge in 2025/26
findings.quote: Discussions are on-going regarding the future of Hammersmith Bridge and the Council is incurring revenue and capital costs at risk until government funding is confirmed.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account cash balances expected to reduce from late 2026/27, potentially requiring external borrowing
findings.detail: The paper states that based on the planned four-year capital programme and expected reduction in cash balances from the latter half of 2026/27 onwards, the HRA may need to actively consider new external borrowing. The HRA is not currently externally borrowing, so this represents a change in financing approach.
findings.matters: The HRA is typically self-financing from rental income. Pressure requiring external borrowing signals either rental income insufficiency or an unusually intense capital programme that depletes reserves, both indicators of financial strain.
findings.figures: Timing: H2 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: For the period 2026/27 to 2029/30, based on the planned four-year capital programme and due to reduced cash balances from the latter half of 2026/27 onwards, the HRA may need to actively consider new external borrowing.

findings.headline: PWLB concessionary borrowing rate expires 31 March 2026, increasing cost of planned capital borrowing
findings.detail: The council currently accesses Public Works Loan Board funding at a concessionary rate (gilt +0.80% for General Fund, +0.40% for HRA). This concessionary rate is scheduled to end on 31 March 2026. While the paper notes this may be extended pending government guidance, expiry would increase the cost of new borrowing. The £161m planned borrowing will be taken after this date.
findings.matters: The cost of the planned £161m borrowing depends on whether concessionary rates continue. If they expire as scheduled, capital financing costs will rise further, compounding affordability pressure.
findings.figures: Concessionary rate: gilt +0.80% (GF) and gilt +0.40% (HRA); expiry date 31 March 2026
findings.quote: All new Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) loans are subject to relevant gilt yields +0.80% (certainty rate) in the General Fund, and gilt yields +0.40% for the Housing Revenue Account (HRA). The concessionary rate is due to end 31 March 2026, however, it is possible this will be extended.

findings.headline: Council forecasts £161m of new borrowing over 2026/27-2027/28 to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The liability benchmark calculation projects that the council will need to borrow £86m in 2026/27 and a further £75m in 2027/28. This borrowing is needed to fund the capital programme as existing under-borrowed position (using reserves and internal resources) becomes exhausted. Gross debt is projected to rise from £426m in 2025/26 to £778m by 2029/30.
findings.matters: Lenders track leverage and borrowing trajectory. The £161m new borrowing combined with declining revenue streams indicates the council will face increasing difficulty financing capital from operating cash flow.
findings.quote: Based on the current calculations, the liability benchmark forecasts that the Council would need to borrow £86m in 2026/27, and a further £75m in 2027/28 (collective £161m requirement).

findings.headline: General Fund capital financing burden doubles from 1.23% to 4.22% of revenue stream by 2029/30
findings.detail: The ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream is forecast to increase substantially over the medium term. This is driven by two factors: increasing minimum revenue provision charges from Civic Campus project completion, and a reducing net revenue stream due to Government implementation of the Fair Funding framework. By 2029/30 the ratio reaches 4.22%, meaning capital financing will consume over 4p in every pound of council revenue.
findings.matters: Lenders assess whether a council can service debt from operating revenues. A doubling of the capital financing burden ratio in four years signals material deterioration in debt servicing capacity relative to income.
findings.quote: From 2026/27 onwards, the ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream for the General Fund increases, primarily for two reasons: firstly an increasing minimum revenue provision charge, with the completion of the Civic Campus project, and secondly a reducing net revenue stream as a result of Government implementing the Fair Funding framework.

findings.headline: £9.5m savings programme includes commercialisation (£5.1m) dependent on income generation and service reconfiguration (£0.2m), representing execution risk
findings.detail: 2026/27 savings of £9.5m break down as: commercialisation/income £5.1m, service rationalisation £3.0m, procurement £0.2m, staffing £0.6m, government-related £0.5m, service reconfiguration £0.2m. Over half relies on new income generation in challenging economic conditions (cost of living crisis, cost pressures on households).
findings.matters: Income-dependent savings are riskier than cost reductions in a weak economy. Council depends on residents and businesses having discretionary spending to pay new/higher fees and charges.
findings.figures: Total service savings £9.5m; commercialisation/income £5.1m (54% of savings); collection fund savings £8.4m
findings.quote: Table 5: Categorisation of savings - Commercialisation / income (5.1); Service rationalisation/budget reduced in line with spend (3.0); Staffing / productivity (0.6)

findings.headline: Contingency budget of only £3m held across MTFS period to cover identified risks in social care, children's services and homelessness
findings.detail: Council holds corporate contingency of approximately £3m budgeted for 2026/27 and across MTFS to manage risks to savings programmes and unforeseen pressures. Paper identifies significant risks in adult social care, children's services, SEND, homelessness and temporary accommodation but contingency is modest relative to risk profile.
findings.matters: Contingency reserves are the buffer against forecast error and demand shocks. A £3m contingency against identified multi-million pressures (£6.8m current year overspend, demand-led services) is tight and leaves limited headroom for adverse variances.
findings.figures: £3m budgeted contingency for 2026/27 and MTFS period; £6.8m current year overspend; £2.1m LGPS pension contribution saving
findings.quote: The Council holds a corporate contingency which can be called upon to manage risks to the agreed budget reduction programme in any one year as well as addressing unforeseen budget pressures which may manifest themselves through the financial year and the medium term. The budgeted level of contingency for 2026/27 and across the remainder of the MTFS is in the region of £3m.

findings.headline: Council Tax debt arrears rose £1.9m and housing rents debt increased £1m between March 2024 and March 2025, with cyber incident adding collection risk
findings.detail: Despite improvements in debt management procedures and ethical collection approaches, Council Tax arrears rose £1.9m and housing rent debt increased £1m year-on-year. Cyber incident in November 2025 'may have an impact on collection rates' creating additional uncertainty into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Growing debt arrears reduce collectible income and signal resident financial stress. Cyber incident adds operational risk to collection processes, potentially reducing income below forecast.
findings.figures: Council Tax arrears increased £1.9m (2024-25); housing rents debt increased £1m; total council debt reduced £7m only due to business rates, benefit overpayments and sundry debt reductions
findings.quote: Council Tax arrears rose by £1.9m and Housing rents debt increased by £1m...The cyber security incident that the Council experienced in November 2025 may have an impact on collection rates.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs remain high with no resolution; national spending exceeds £2.8bn and projected to rise further without subsidy reform
findings.detail: Council budgets £36.8m gross for temporary accommodation (General Fund). Paper notes national spending exceeded £2.8bn in 2024/25 and 'projected to rise further without subsidy reform.' Council has mitigation strategies but acknowledges continuing pressure from homelessness, private rent inflation, and affordability crisis.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a demand-led cost driven by national housing shortage and private rental market. Without external intervention, costs will continue to rise. This directly impacts council affordability.
findings.figures: £36.8m gross cost budgeted for temporary accommodation; national spending exceeded £2.8bn in 2024/25
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation – costs remain significant, with national spending exceeding £2.8bn in 2024/25 and projected to rise further without subsidy reform

findings.headline: Adult social care demand pressures persist; free home care provision for 1,623 residents is cost pressure not matched by funding growth
findings.detail: Gross Adult Social Care expenditure budget is £115.3m (net £74.4m). The council provides free home care for older residents—a unique provision supporting 1,623 residents delivering 1.164m annual care hours. Council continues to absorb demographic and provider cost pressures while demographic trends show ageing populations driving increased demand and complexity.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a high-cost, demand-driven service. Free home care is a policy choice that creates an ongoing cost pressure. Ageing demographics mean this cost will continue to rise.
findings.figures: £115.3m gross budget; £40.5m on residential/nursing (459 residents); £19.6m home care (1,623 residents delivering 1.164m annual hours); £13.8m supported living (285 residents)
findings.quote: We are the only council in the country to provide free Home Care for those who need it, helping 1,623 residents who would otherwise have to pay for expensive care at a time when they are most vulnerable.

findings.headline: Cyber security incident with unquantified short and medium-term cost implications from legacy shared systems
findings.detail: Council experienced a cyber security incident in November 2025 affecting legacy systems shared with a neighbouring council. The council successfully isolated its network but acknowledges unquantified future costs. Impact on collection rates is unknown but flagged as a risk to be clarified in early 2026.
findings.matters: Cyber incidents can have material financial consequences including remediation, system replacement, and operational disruption. Unquantified costs create budget unpredictability.
findings.figures: Incident date November 2025; collection rate impact to be assessed in early 2026
findings.quote: The council has been affected by a cyber security incident in a neighbouring council with shared legacy systems. We were able to successfully isolate and safeguard our network. However, it is likely there will be short and medium cost implications to be reported in the future.

findings.headline: Current year forecast overspend of £6.8m (reducing to £2.2m with mitigating actions), indicating pressure on 2025/26 delivery
findings.detail: Month 6 Corporate Revenue Monitoring Report forecasts current year (2025/26) overspend of £6.8m, reducing only to £2.2m if current mitigating actions are delivered and contingency budgets are used. This suggests demand-led pressures are materialising despite management actions and indicates reliance on one-off contingency measures.
findings.matters: Current-year overspends signal that forecasting assumptions may be optimistic and demand pressures are real. Reliance on contingency to close gaps reduces buffer for 2026/27 unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Month 6 forecast overspend £6.8m; forecast £2.2m after mitigating actions and use of contingency
findings.quote: The latest current year Corporate Revenue Monitoring Report (month 6) forecasts an overspend of £6.8m (reducing to £2.2mm should current mitigating actions be delivered, and the use of contingency budgets).

findings.headline: SEND historic deficits represent an unquantified financial risk; government taking on future costs centrally from 2028/29 but prior liability unclear
findings.detail: Government confirms it will take on future SEND costs centrally from 2028/29 onwards, relieving councils of statutory override pressures. However, the paper explicitly states 'There is currently no clarity on historic deficits, which is a major financial risk for Councils.' This means prior-year accumulated deficits from SEND overspends may remain the council's liability.
findings.matters: SEND is demand-led and high-cost. Unresolved historic deficits could represent a hidden contingent liability. The uncertainty prevents accurate long-term financial forecasting.
findings.figures: 3,602 children in H&F with SEND support needs; 1,858 with Education and Health Care Plans; £74.5m budgeted for education and SEND (2026/27)
findings.quote: Government to take on future SEND costs centrally from 2028/29, relieving councils of statutory override pressures. There is currently no clarity on historic deficits, which is a major financial risk for Councils.

findings.headline: Council forecasts funding cuts of up to 12% by 2028/29 with transitional relief ending, creating medium-term sustainability risk
findings.detail: The multi-year settlement provides transitional funding protection at 95% of core spending power for 2026/27, but thereafter transitional funding reduces by £150 per Band D equivalent annually across the council tax base. Fair Funding reform is forecast to reduce funding by up to 12% by 2028/29. The council acknowledges this requires 'considerably sooner' absorption of reductions than previously modelled.
findings.matters: The cliff-edge removal of transitional funding within three years creates a material and near-term financial planning challenge. This directly impacts council borrowing requirements and reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: Transitional funding £6.0m (2026/27), declining £150 per Band D equivalent in subsequent years; forecast funding cuts up to 12% by 2028/29
findings.quote: The organisation will need to ensure it is ready to absorb these annual funding reductions, which will now present considerably sooner than previously modelled (because of less transitional funding). The three-year settlement information is factored into the Medium Term Financial Strategy at Appendix B.

findings.headline: Business Rates tariff quadruples due to Fair Funding reform, reducing retained business rates income and increasing government payments
findings.detail: The tariff Hammersmith & Fulham pays to Government increases from £12.8m to £53.6m in 2026/27 as a result of Fair Funding Review 2.0 and business rates reset. From £300m gross rates collected in the borough, the council retains only 10%. This structural change creates a £23.5m decrease in combined government grants and retained business rates funding year-on-year.
findings.matters: This represents a material reduction in funding available for service delivery, independent of council performance or choices. Lenders need to understand whether this creates unsustainable pressures over the medium term.
findings.figures: Tariff increases from £12.8m to £53.6m; core spending power decreases £11.3m (4.7%); combined funding decrease of £23.5m
findings.quote: The tariff H&F pays to Government quadruples, from £12.8m in 2025/26 to £53.6m in 2026/27. This means that from an indicative gross rates collectible within the borough of £300m, Hammersmith and Fulham Council retains 10% of this.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Medium term financial forecast
findings.headline: Cyber security incident in November 2025 with unquantified financial impact
findings.detail: The council suffered a cyber incident in late November 2025. At the time the budget was prepared, the cost impact across both spending and lost income could not be quantified. The council states impact will be assessed in early 2026.
findings.matters: Cyber incidents can result in substantial unbudgeted costs, service interruption, and income losses. The council is acknowledging it cannot yet assess the exposure, which is a disclosure risk in itself.
findings.figures: Cost and income impact unquantified as at budget preparation date
findings.quote: The Council had cyber security incident in late November 2025. At the point of the budget report being prepared, it has not been possible to fully quantify impact, across costs and income, at the point that this report was being prepared, but this will be done in early 2026 when we will be in a clearer place to update information.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Medium term financial forecast
findings.headline: SEND statutory override ends March 2028 with no confirmed funding solution from government
findings.detail: The Statutory Override allows councils to borrow to cover high needs DSG deficits. It expires in March 2028. The government has indicated SEND reform is coming in early 2026 and councils will not be expected to use general funds for deficits after 2028, but has not yet confirmed how these deficits will be funded or what support councils will receive.
findings.matters: If the government does not provide adequate funding or an alternative mechanism, the council will face a structural gap on top of the already-forecasted £57m+ deficit. The timeline is now visible and the uncertainty is real.
findings.figures: Statutory Override ends March 2028; SEND reform plans to be presented early 2026
findings.quote: The Government has indicated it will be presenting plans for SEND reform early in 2026. The direction of travel is that local authorities will not be expected to use general funds to cover DSG High Needs Block deficits after the Statutory Override ends in March 2028. The Government has stated that it recognises that local authorities will need support for historic and accruing deficits and details of this support will be provided through the Local Government Finance Settlement, though this has not yet been provided.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Medium term financial forecast
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs are escalating with B&B annexe use up 143% in eight months
findings.detail: The council now houses 1,525 households in temporary accommodation, 62% of them in other boroughs. B&B annexe placements — the most expensive type — grew from 151 households in April 2024 to 367 by December 2025. The council admits it had to use this accommodation because supply of cheaper options could not keep pace with homelessness demand of 2,981 households in 2024/25.
findings.matters: TA is a volatile, high-cost service growing faster than the council can secure cheaper alternatives. Costs are already embedded in the budget but the trajectory suggests further pressure is baked in.
findings.figures: 1,525 households in TA as at 1 November 2025; B&B annexe 151 (Apr-24) to 367 (Dec-25); 2,981 households approached as homeless in 2024/25
findings.quote: the supply of TA in -borough is limited, and 62% of households are placed in TA across other London boroughs

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Medium term financial forecast
findings.headline: Central government transitional funding of £34m ceases in 2028/29, deepening the funding cliff
findings.detail: Hammersmith and Fulham receives transitional relief because the funding reform redistributes resources towards more deprived areas, cutting inner London boroughs' core grant. This protection lasts three years only. Once transitional funding ends, the council faces full exposure to the reduced baseline.
findings.matters: The council is dependent on time-limited central support that explicitly ends. No replacement funding has been announced. This makes the 2028/29 position structural, not cyclical.
findings.figures: £34m transitional funding to 2028/29; funding reform forecast to reduce core grant for inner London boroughs
findings.quote: Because of the Government's aims to redistribute resources towards areas of higher deprivation, inner London boroughs including Hammersmith and Fulham , are forecast to receive significantly less funding across the duration of this MTFS. Hammersmith and Fulham is eligible for transitional funding relief over the three years to 2028/29, amounting to £34m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Medium term financial forecast
findings.headline: A budget gap of £31.4m emerges in 2027/28 and doubles to £57.3m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget is balanced, but this relies on one-off funding from collection fund releases. From 2027/28 onwards, the cumulative effect of grant funding reductions, inflationary pressures, and service demand creates escalating deficits. The pessimistic scenario forecasts deficits as high as £69m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A council with deficits of this magnitude cannot be sustained from reserves alone and will be forced into significant service reductions, asset disposals, or unsustainable borrowing within two years.
findings.figures: 2027/28 gap £31.4m, 2028/29 gap £57.3m; pessimistic scenario 2028/29 gap £69.0m
findings.quote: The table above presents an initial assessment of the budget gap for the 2027 /28 financial year of just over £31.4m, with the material elements of this gap being the reversal of one -off funding within the 2026/27 budget

findings.headline: Detailed asset management strategy cost implications still being finalised with explicit risk of budget overrun in 2026/27 and beyond
findings.detail: The 10-year plan budgets £0.94bn for repairs and investment, but the council states the detailed asset management strategy is still being finalised. It explicitly flags risk that actual costs will exceed the proposed budget. Compliance-driven works (Building Safety Act, Fire Safety Act) may require additional spending not yet quantified.
findings.matters: Undefined capital cost exposure creates budget uncertainty; if compliance works cost more than budgeted, the council must either cut services, borrow more, or defer other investment
findings.figures: £0.94bn investment over 10 years; £25.1m repairs and maintenance budgeted 2026/27; £675.1m total 10-year capital expenditure planned
findings.quote: Whilst the full cost implications of implementing the Council's HRA 10-year Business Plan are still being determined (the asset management strategy is currently being finalised), there is a risk that costs are in excess of the proposed budget for 2026/27 and in the longer term.

findings.headline: Welfare reform risks including Universal Credit migration creating £1.3m bad debt exposure and potential faster-than-expected benefit claim transfers
findings.detail: The council faces risk from government welfare reform. Universal Credit migration for existing claims was delayed by Covid and is expected to complete by December 2025, but there is explicit risk of faster migration than anticipated. Bad debt provision for rents has been increased to £1.3m for 2026/27.
findings.matters: If Universal Credit migration accelerates or if tenants experience delays in receiving benefit payments, rent collection could deteriorate rapidly; the £1.3m bad debt provision may prove insufficient, threatening budget balance
findings.figures: £1.3m bad debt provision for rents in 2026/27; Universal Credit migration expected complete by December 2025
findings.quote: The HRA faces multiple financial risks including those arising from the Government's programme of Welfare Reform which continues to represent a risk to the Council's ability to collect rental income and may result in increased bad debt charges to the HRA. There is a risk that the migration of tenants to Universal Credit moves at a faster pace than expected.

findings.headline: Rent income increase of 4.8% will not fully offset accumulated inflationary cost pressures in 2026/27 and beyond
findings.detail: The government-mandated 4.8% rent increase (CPI+1%) generates £4.1m additional income but the council explicitly states this will not recover inflationary pressures that have accumulated in recent years. This creates a structural gap: if cost inflation exceeds rent growth, service quality must decline or reserves must be drawn.
findings.matters: Rent income capped below actual cost inflation means the council cannot grow income proportionally to expenditure; this forces either service reductions or reserve depletion over time
findings.figures: 4.8% rent increase from April 2026; additional rent income £4.1m; pay inflation 2.5% (£0.7m); contracted services inflation £0.9m
findings.quote: The rent increase will be set at 4.8% from April 2026 (in line with national rent policy). The income that will be generated will not fully offset the inflationary cost pressures accumulated in recent years.

findings.headline: General reserves of £5.9m (less than 3.5 weeks of gross rental income) for 11,880 homes and £1.4bn asset base provides thin buffer
findings.detail: Minimum reserves of £5.9m are maintained after reductions in previous years to fund capital investment. This represents only 3.5 weeks of HRA gross rental income for a large stock requiring ongoing compliance investment and exposed to welfare reform impacts.
findings.matters: Thin reserves reduce ability to absorb unexpected costs (major repairs failures, audit challenges, faster welfare reform impacts, income loss) without immediate service cuts or additional borrowing
findings.figures: £5.9m general reserve as at 31 March 2025; equivalent to less than 3.5 weeks of HRA gross rental income
findings.quote: The HRA general reserve as at 31 March 2025 was £5.9m. This is equivalent to less than three and a half weeks' of HRA gross rental income.

findings.headline: £4.1m deficit in 2022/23 now eliminated but 2026/27 budget depends on delivering £3.9m savings programme to remain balanced
findings.detail: The council had a substantial HRA deficit three years ago that required correction. The current budget does not generate surplus: it relies on execution of £3.9m cumulative savings by 2026/27 to avoid reserve drawdown. If savings slip, the budget immediately goes into deficit.
findings.matters: Recent deficit history shows budget vulnerability; ongoing dependency on savings delivery creates execution risk that could force service cuts or reserve depletion if targets are missed
findings.figures: £4.1m base deficit in 2022/23; cumulative savings of £3.9m required by 2026/27
findings.quote: The financial position of the HRA has improved considerably from 2022/23 (the base deficit of £4.1m in that year has been fully eliminated from 2024/25 onwards).

findings.headline: Debt servicing costs rising by £4.0m in 2026/27, with total borrowing planned of £281.1m over 10 years and debt-to-value ratio reaching 43%
findings.detail: Higher interest rates combined with increased borrowing to support compliance works drive significant additional interest costs. The 10-year plan shows debt outstanding rising from £594m in 2026/27 to £885m by 2035/36. Debt to property value increases from 40% to 43%, approaching lending thresholds.
findings.matters: Growing debt servicing costs consume income that could otherwise fund repairs and maintenance; rising debt ratios narrow future borrowing headroom if revenues weaken
findings.figures: £4.0m increase in debt servicing costs for 2026/27; £281.1m total borrowing planned over 10 years; debt outstanding £594m rising to £885m; debt to property value 40% rising to 43%
findings.quote: Higher interest rates, together with an increase in borrowing to support the compliance-based capital programme, are expected to result in a significant increase in debt servicing costs for 2026/27 of £4.0m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – Grant Thornton UK LLP Audit Findings Report (ISA260) (Main Financial Statements 2024-25)
findings.headline: Pension fund asset understatement of £3.993m identified post-accounts preparation due to late valuation updates
findings.detail: The pension fund audit identified that fund assets were understated by £3.993m because updated valuations were received after the Council's accounts were prepared. Although this does not impact the recognized pension liability due to IFRIC 14 asset ceiling restrictions, it indicates a control gap in obtaining timely pension fund data and suggests the Council's closing pension position may not reflect fully updated valuations.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are a material long-term obligation. Late receipt of valuation data and post-accounts discoveries suggest control weakness in pension fund data collection and timing.
findings.figures: £3.993m asset understatement in pension fund, £37.1m net pension liability overall
findings.quote: Additionally, the Pension Fund audit noted an understatement of assets amounting to £3.993 million, due to updated valuations received after the preparation of the accounts. While this does not impact the pension liability in the financial statements due to the application of IFRIC 14...

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – Grant Thornton UK LLP Audit Findings Report (ISA260) (Main Financial Statements 2024-25)
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision increased to £13.8m in 2024-25 with £10.2m now classified as lease charges under IFRS 16
findings.detail: MRP charge increased from prior year standard of £3.6m to total of £13.8m. IFRS 16 implementation requires £10.2m of lease payments to be reclassified from direct General Fund charges to MRP charges, effectively increasing the council's annual debt repayment burden. While the auditor confirms impact on General Fund remains consistent, this represents a material increase in capital financing requirements.
findings.matters: For a lender, increasing MRP charges reduce discretionary resources available and indicate a higher capital financing burden, affecting debt sustainability ratios.
findings.figures: £13.8m total MRP (2024-25), £3.6m standard MRP element, £10.2m IFRS 16 lease payment charge
findings.quote: The overall increase to £13.8m reflects the adoption of IFRS 16. Under this new standard, £10.2m of lease payments are now treated as a charge to MRP. Previously, these payments were charged directly to the General Fund

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – Grant Thornton UK LLP Audit Findings Report (ISA260) (Main Financial Statements 2024-25)
findings.headline: Elector objection to accounts on pensions received during public inspection; audit cannot be certified until objection review is complete
findings.detail: A valid elector raised an objection relating to pensions during the statutory public inspection period. The auditor is reviewing this objection but does not expect completion prior to finishing audit work. The audit cannot be formally certified under the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 until this matter is resolved. While the audit opinion remains unmodified, the certification remains open.
findings.matters: An elector challenge to pension accounting may indicate public concern or dispute over accuracy of pension liability recognition. Unresolved public objections create reputational and potential regulatory risk.
findings.figures: 1 elector objection raised and pending review
findings.quote: Within the Public inspection period an objection to the accounts was received. This objection was raised by a valid elector and within the objection window, relating to Pensions. We will not be able to certify the 2024-25 audit until we have completed our work on this objection.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – Grant Thornton UK LLP Audit Findings Report (ISA260) (Main Financial Statements 2024-25)
findings.headline: HRA council dwellings portfolio of £1,266m (40% of property assets) relies on indexation between five-year revaluation cycles rather than annual inspections
findings.detail: The 12,018-unit council dwellings portfolio was valued at £1,266.4m at 31 March 2025 (down £92m from prior year). Between five-yearly full revaluations, values are adjusted using indexation applied to beacon properties, but inspections are not conducted annually. The auditor noted that for such a large portfolio, there is risk that market conditions could diverge materially from indexed assumptions, and recommended moving to annual sample inspection methodology.
findings.matters: A lender assessing collateral and financial sustainability needs confidence that the largest single asset class is accurately valued. Heavy reliance on indexation rather than market evidence creates estimation risk.
findings.figures: £1,266.4m council dwellings valuation, down £92m from prior year, 12,018 properties in portfolio, 86% of OLB assets revalued in 2024-25
findings.quote: Although this is in line with the instructions sent to the valuer... for a portfolio of council dwellings as large as the Councils' (£1.2bn in 2024/25) the current methodology could be updated... every year from the beacon population of properties a certain percentage gets inspected with comparable data used to determine its valuation

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – Grant Thornton UK LLP Audit Findings Report (ISA260) (Main Financial Statements 2024-25)
findings.headline: £65.9m combined investment and capital commitment to West King Street civic campus joint venture with completion expected in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Council has £25m equity invested in West King Street Renewal LLP (50/50 partnership with A2 Dominion) and £40.9m of capital debtors relating to prepayments for construction. The auditor reclassified £40.9m from long-term to short-term debtors expecting completion in the upcoming financial year. The JV has recorded a £6.2m provision for penalty clauses that the Council may exercise but has not yet recognized as a debtor, though management notes it will evaluate whether to exercise this option.
findings.matters: This represents the Council's single largest capital commitment. A lender needs confidence in the recoverability of £65.9m of capital and ability to complete a complex development with a joint venture partner.
findings.figures: £25m equity investment, £40.9m capital debtor reclassified to short-term, £6.2m potential penalty provision in JV, £2.6m expected profit share on exit
findings.quote: The Council has made these payments to the JV following surveyor reviews and completion statements. However, The Council has not recognised this balance as Property, Plant and Equipment, based on its assessment that it does not yet have control over the asset.

findings.headline: Liquidity and HRA contingency levels flagged for attention
findings.detail: Among four improvement recommendations, auditors specifically identify liquidity and the level of contingencies held in the HRA as requiring review. This suggests working capital or cash management concerns.
findings.matters: Liquidity concerns indicate potential cash flow issues; HRA contingency adequacy affects the council's ability to absorb housing-related shocks.
findings.figures: Two of four improvement recommendations focus on liquidity and HRA contingencies
findings.quote: these relate to the HRA (level of contingencies, stock condition work), our liquidity and reporting our regular Treasury reports to Audit Committee in addition to Cabinet

findings.headline: Council-wide governance assessed as amber
findings.detail: The auditors assessed the council as amber on governance arrangements, indicating control or oversight weaknesses. The specific issues are detailed in the full auditor report, not this summary.
findings.matters: Governance weaknesses affect financial management quality and control environment; lenders view this as a risk indicator.
findings.figures: Governance: Amber
findings.quote: the external auditors have assessed the Council as 'green' on financial sustainability and 'amber' for governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account rated amber on financial sustainability, while general fund is green
findings.detail: The HRA received an amber rating on financial sustainability, in contrast to the general fund which was green. The HRA also received amber ratings on governance and improving economy/efficiency/effectiveness, suggesting housing finance faces specific pressures absent from the general fund.
findings.matters: HRA finance constraints affect the council's overall financial flexibility and borrowing capacity; lenders assess this separately from general fund strength.
findings.figures: Financial sustainability: HRA Amber; General fund Green. Governance: Amber (HRA). Improving economy/efficiency/effectiveness: Amber (HRA)
findings.quote: Financial sustainability - HRA  Amber

news_drafts.headline: Pension fund has written off overpayments and is working to recover further outstanding overpayment funds
news_drafts.lead: Overpayment write-offs and recovery issues indicate control weaknesses in pension administration and represent financial losses absorbed by the fund; ongoing recovery efforts suggest a systemic problem rather than isolated incidents

news_drafts.headline: Helpdesk service performance deteriorated in Q1 with longer wait times and higher call abandonment
news_drafts.lead: Degrading service metrics during a period of stated resource constraints could indicate that the council's outsourced pension administration is beginning to strain under demand, risking further member dissatisfaction and operational failures

news_drafts.headline: Pension administration service faces resource constraints that are slowing resolution of issues
news_drafts.lead: Under-resourced pension administration could compromise the council's ability to meet regulatory obligations (such as McCloud remedies or Pensions Dashboard connectivity) and could create financial exposure if issues are not resolved promptly
